I think at least part of it has to do with graphics being capable of looking very pretty even if they aren't highly advanced. Because of this, many early 3d games tend to age pretty poorly (because the graphic quality of 3d engines made enormous advancements over the years to the point that we have almost photo-realistic graphics nowadays), while games that rely on sprites and/or pixel art have not advanced very much, in the technical sense.

Or, put differently: Those games that age well typically still look good because the developers pulled the best they could do with the (back then fairly limited) graphical tools at their disposal. Ingenuity wins the day.
2D games seem to age well for the most part. I got this question when I tried to play my n64, and it doesn't look very nice on an hdtv.

Consider that that the N64 was notorious for its very limited texture storage space. Developers (I'm especially thinking of Rareware) had to pull off all sorts of technical shenanigans with the game's textures, which are the only reason why games like Conquer's Bad Fur Day looked comparatively good when compared to contemporary playstation games.

Some games are just made well, others aren't.

Also, the art style and nature of the content itself has something to do with it. Jet fighters, for example, are particularly easy to render, and low poly models look fine from a distance, so the old PS2 Ace Combat games hold up really well.
